claims.text: Undoped single-phase ZrB2 conventionally requires sintering above 2300 °C.
Approximately 2 wt% TiC can act as a reactive sintering aid in ZrB2.
Adding approximately 2 wt% TiC will enable ZrB2 densification at 2100–2150 °C.
The proposed processing temperature is approximately 150–200 °C below 2300 °C.
TiC reacts at ZrB2 grain boundaries during sintering.
The TiC-related grain-boundary reaction generates a localized transient liquid phase.
The transient liquid phase enhances local mass transport.
The transient liquid phase promotes grain-boundary diffusion.
Enhanced mass transport and grain-boundary diffusion accelerate densification at reduced temperature.
TiC-assisted sintering produces a denser ZrB2 microstructure with fewer and smaller residual pores.
Reduced residual porosity improves the microstructural integrity of the ceramic.
Improved microstructural integrity increases resistance to defect or hole formation during prolonged liquid plating bath exposure.
Improved microstructural integrity increases resistance to chemical attack during prolonged liquid plating bath exposure.
At the reduced sintering temperature, TiC-doped ZrB2 will achieve nearly equivalent densification to conventionally prepared ZrB2.
At the reduced sintering temperature, TiC-doped ZrB2 will achieve nearly equivalent mechanical strength to conventionally prepared ZrB2.
TiC-doped ZrB2 will exhibit fewer holes and less long-term corrosion or degradation in a liquid plating bath than conventionally prepared ZrB2.
Conventionally prepared ZrB2 typically has higher residual porosity and is prone to microstructural damage during prolonged liquid plating bath exposure.

contradictions.description: The stated comparator is conventionally prepared ZrB2 sintered above 2300 °C, but the experiment sinters both the undoped control and TiC-doped material at 2100–2150 °C. The resulting undoped control is not the stated conventional baseline, even though the falsification rule describes the comparison as being against conventional ZrB2.
